It is a variant of PRIM-001 that exploits the loop structure to show that data from previous iterations persists in the buffer and is leaked by puts(). Both PRIM-001 and PRIM-002 exploit the same root cause (no NUL termination + unbounded puts) but from different angles.

source.root_cause: The INFO_LEAK from BUG-002 (PRIM-001) leaks the stack canary. With the canary known, the stack buffer overflow from BUG-001 can be exploited: send 0x80=128 bytes with the correct canary at offset 0x68 and a controlled return address at offset 0x78. The canary check passes, and ret jumps to the attacker-controlled return address.
source.description: PRIM-001 leaks the canary via puts(). The leaked canary is then used in a 0x80-byte overflow payload: 0x68 bytes filler + 8 bytes correct canary + 8 bytes saved RBP + 8 bytes return address. The canary check at 0x12a1 passes (canary matches fs:0x28), and ret at 0x12b6 jumps to the attacker-controlled return address at [rbp+0x8].

chain: BUG-002
INFO_LEAK: canary leaked via puts() after overwriting NUL low byte
Attacker reconstructs full 8-byte canary as 0x00 || leaked_bytes[1..7]
BUG-001: read(0, buf, 0x80) overflows buffer by 24 bytes
Overflow payload: 0x68 filler + correct canary + saved RBP + target return address
Canary check passes (canary matches fs:0x28)
ret at 0x12b6 jumps to attacker-controlled [rbp+0x8]
RIP_CONTROL: return address fully controlled by attacker

controlled_element.what: Return address at [rbp+0x8] (bytes 0x78-0x7f of the 0x80-byte read input)
controlled_element.how: 1. Leak canary via PRIM-001 (send 0x69 bytes, observe puts() output for canary bytes 1-7). 2. Construct 0x80-byte payload: 0x68 bytes filler + p64(canary) + p64(fake_rbp) + p64(target_rip). 3. Send payload via read() in the loop. 4. Send '--\0' to exit loop. 5. Canary check passes, ret jumps to target_rip.

preconditions.description: Canary must be leaked first via PRIM-001 (requires one loop iteration to leak, then another to overflow)
preconditions.necessity: Without the correct canary value, __stack_chk_fail is triggered at 0x12b0, aborting the process before ret

preconditions.description: The overflow payload must be exactly 0x80=128 bytes to reach the return address at [rbp+0x8]
preconditions.necessity: The return address is at offset 0x78 from the buffer start; sending fewer bytes does not overwrite it

preconditions.description: The canary must be placed at the correct offset (0x68) in the overflow payload
preconditions.necessity: The canary is at [rbp-0x8] = buffer + 0x68; placing it at the wrong offset causes canary check failure

preconditions.description: The loop must be exited after the overflow by sending '--\0' (with NUL terminator to ensure strcmp matches)
preconditions.necessity: Without exiting the loop, the function never reaches the canary check and ret instruction

preconditions.description: The '--\0' exit string must have a NUL terminator because read() does not NUL-terminate; without it, strcmp(buf, '--') sees residual data after '--' and does not match
preconditions.necessity: The buffer retains data from the overflow payload; without NUL after '--', strcmp compares '--DDDD...' with '--' and does not match, causing the loop to continue indefinitely

alias_key_findings.expression: canary at [rbp-0x8] = buffer[0x68..0x6f], return address at [rbp+0x8] = buffer[0x78..0x7f]
alias_key_findings.alias: The 0x80-byte read input maps directly to: buffer[0x00..0x67]=filler, buffer[0x68..0x6f]=canary, buffer[0x70..0x77]=saved RBP, buffer[0x78..0x7f]=return address
alias_key_findings.implication: By controlling all 0x80 bytes of input, the attacker controls the canary (must match fs:0x28), saved RBP, and return address. The canary is known from PRIM-001's leak, so the canary check passes, and ret jumps to the controlled return address.

mitigations.name: Stack Canary
mitigations.primitive_impact: The stack canary is bypassed by leaking it via PRIM-001 (puts() info leak). The leaked canary is placed in the overflow payload at the correct offset, causing the canary check to pass. This is a complete canary bypass.

mitigations.name: PIE/ASLR
mitigations.primitive_impact: PIE/ASLR randomizes code addresses, but the RIP_CONTROL primitive is verified with fixed invalid addresses (0x4141..., 0xdeadbeef..., 0x4242...) that cause SIGSEGV. In a real exploit (S4), the attacker would need to leak PIE base or libc base to redirect to a valid address. The primitive itself (RIP = attacker-controlled value) is verified regardless of ASLR.

mitigations.name: NX
mitigations.primitive_impact: NX prevents executing shellcode on the stack, but does not prevent RIP_CONTROL itself. The attacker can redirect to existing code (ROP) but cannot execute injected code.

mitigations.name: Full RELRO
mitigations.primitive_impact: Full RELRO prevents GOT overwrite, but does not affect the stack-based RIP_CONTROL primitive.

mitigations.name: CET (IBT+SHSTK)
mitigations.primitive_impact: CET Shadow Stack (SHSTK) would detect the return address overwrite and raise a fault. However, CET is enabled in the ELF but may not be enforced at runtime depending on kernel/hardware support. The dynamic verification shows SIGSEGV (not CET fault), suggesting CET is not enforced in this environment.

evidence.description: Canary check: mov rax,[rbp-0x8]; xor rax,fs:0x28; je 0x12b5; call __stack_chk_fail. If canary matches, execution continues to leave;ret at 0x12b5-0x12b6. The ret instruction pops [rbp+0x8] (which was overwritten by the overflow) into RIP.

Dynamic verification: 3 separate runs with different target_rip values (0x4141414141414141, 0xdeadbeefcafebabe, 0x4242424242424242). All 3 runs produced exit code -11 (SIGSEGV), proving: (1) canary was correctly leaked and reconstructed (no SIGABRT), (2) ret jumped to the attacker-specified address (SIGSEGV at invalid address). The canary was different in each run (ASLR re-randomizes canary per process), but was correctly leaked each time.

verification_result.details: PRIM-003 VERIFIED: 3 runs with different target_rip values. Run 1: canary=0x404214fa799e3300, target=0x4141414141414141, exit=-11 (SIGSEGV). Run 2: canary=0x72a9893f5537b500, target=0xdeadbeefcafebabe, exit=-11 (SIGSEGV). Run 3: canary=0xd5e9b4aa29b8100, target=0x4242424242424242, exit=-11 (SIGSEGV). All 3 runs: canary check passed (no SIGABRT), ret jumped to attacker-specified address (SIGSEGV). This proves: (1) canary leak is correct, (2) canary bypass works, (3) return address is fully attacker-controlled.

primitives.notes: PRIM-003 is an INDIRECT primitive: it depends on PRIM-001 (canary leak) as a precondition. The chain is: BUG-002 (info leak) → canary leaked → BUG-001 (buffer overflow) → canary bypassed → return address overwritten → RIP_CONTROL. The '--\0' exit string (with NUL terminator) is critical: without the NUL, strcmp(buf, '--') sees residual overflow data after '--' and does not match, causing the loop to continue indefinitely. CET Shadow Stack is declared in the ELF but appears not enforced at runtime (SIGSEGV, not CET fault).
